items.prompt: What is the "virtual DOM"?
choices: A lightweight, in-memory representation of what the UI should currently look like, compared against the previous version to compute minimal real DOM changes
A backup copy of the real DOM that the server keeps in case the client crashes mid-render
A separate DOM tree the browser maintains only for computing print stylesheets
The browser's internal cache of resolved CSS specificity rules for faster re-renders
items.explanation: The virtual DOM is an in-memory comparison target used to compute the smallest set of real DOM changes needed — not a server backup, print-specific tree, or CSS mechanism.

items.prompt: Why do frameworks compare a virtual DOM instead of applying every change directly to the real DOM?
choices: To compute the minimal set of real DOM changes needed, since real DOM operations are more expensive than in-memory comparisons
Because direct DOM manipulation from JavaScript is disabled by default in most modern browsers
Because CSS rules fail to apply correctly unless a virtual DOM comparison runs first
Because the real DOM only accepts a single batch of changes per page load cycle
items.explanation: The virtual DOM exists specifically to minimize costly real DOM operations by computing the smallest necessary change set first.

items.prompt: Does the virtual DOM ever get drawn directly on the screen?
choices: No — it's only an in-memory comparison target; the browser never renders it directly
Yes — it's a special layer the browser paints before the real DOM
Only when the page has fewer than 100 elements
Yes, but only while the page is loading
items.explanation: The virtual DOM never touches the screen by itself — it's purely a tool for computing what the real DOM needs to change to.

items.prompt: After a virtual DOM diff finishes, what does the framework apply to the real DOM?
choices: Only the specific minimal set of changes the diff determined were actually needed
The entire new virtual DOM tree, replacing the real DOM wholesale every time
Nothing — the virtual DOM tree becomes the new real DOM automatically
A randomly selected subset of the changes, resolved on the next render
items.explanation: The whole point of diffing first is to apply only the minimal necessary changes, not to replace everything.

items.prompt: Which is generally cheaper: comparing two in-memory virtual DOM trees, or mutating the real DOM?
choices: Comparing two in-memory trees is generally cheaper than real DOM mutations
Mutating the real DOM is always cheaper, which is why virtual DOM diffing is unnecessary overhead
They cost exactly the same amount of work in every browser
Neither — cost depends entirely on the user's internet connection speed
items.explanation: In-memory comparisons are cheap; real DOM mutations can trigger layout/paint work, which is exactly what diffing first is meant to minimize.

items.prompt: What is the virtual DOM compared against to figure out what changed?
choices: The previous version of the virtual DOM itself, from the last render
A hardcoded list of 'safe' changes defined by the framework's authors
The user's browser history for the current page
A snapshot of the server's database at the time of the last request
items.explanation: Diffing compares the new virtual DOM tree against the one computed on the previous render to find exactly what's different.

items.prompt: Is the virtual DOM a backup of the real DOM, kept in case the client crashes?
choices: No — it's a comparison target used to compute minimal changes, not a crash-recovery backup
Yes — that's specifically what it's for
Yes, but only in frameworks that support offline mode
It's a backup of the server's rendered HTML, not the client's DOM
items.explanation: The virtual DOM's job is enabling cheap comparison before touching the real DOM — it has nothing to do with crash recovery or backups.

items.prompt: In one sentence, what problem does the virtual-DOM-plus-diffing pattern solve?
choices: It minimizes expensive real DOM operations by first computing the smallest necessary change in a cheap, in-memory representation
It eliminates the need for the browser to ever recalculate layout
It guarantees the UI never contains a rendering bug
It replaces the need for a server entirely
items.explanation: The pattern's purpose is specifically to keep real DOM work to the minimum necessary, by doing the comparison somewhere cheaper first.

items.prompt: A junior developer proposes skipping the virtual DOM entirely and re-rendering the whole real DOM subtree from scratch on every state change, arguing "it's simpler." What's the main performance cost this introduces that the virtual DOM pattern exists to avoid?
choices: It reapplies far more real DOM operations (and triggers more reflow/repaint) than the minimal set actually needed, since nothing computes what truly changed first
Nothing — modern browsers optimize this automatically regardless of how the change is applied
It would only be a problem for pages with fewer than 10 elements

items.explanation: Re-rendering from scratch skips the step that virtual DOM diffing exists for — figuring out the minimal real DOM change — so every update pays the full cost of rebuilding and reapplying far more than necessary.
items.reflection: The virtual-DOM idea — compute the cheapest possible change in a fast, disposable representation before touching the expensive, real one — shows up outside UI frameworks too: database query planners build a plan in memory before touching disk, and compilers build an AST before emitting real machine code.
